This report describes how the *Follow the Gold* scrollytelling narrative should be evaluated, what informal evaluation was carried out during development, and what the remaining gaps are. The framing follows the three value dimensions used throughout the course documentation (cognitive, communicative, experiential) and the *narrative-visualization* lens introduced by @segel_narrative_2010.

A scrollytelling piece cannot be evaluated the same way a dashboard can. The standard task-completion / time-on-task / number-of-clicks instruments assume a reader who is looking up an answer. *Follow the Gold*'s reader is being **told** an answer; the right question is not "did they find the data point?" but "did the argument land?". The evaluation framework below is structured around that distinction.

## Evaluation Setup

### Evaluation Objectives

The product is evaluated against the success criteria stated in the [Project Charta](project_charta.qmd) and the design discipline laid out in the [Visualization Design Report](viz_design_report.qmd). Each criterion is mapped to one of the three value dimensions.

| Success criterion | Value dimension | What "passing" looks like |
|---|---|---|
| Reader understands the driving question in 30 s of arrival | Cognitive | When asked *"what is this page about?"* after 30 s of free reading, the reader names something in the family of "who actually bought gold in 2022" / "is gold really the inflation hedge". |
| Beat 2 disconfirmation is visible on the chart alone | Cognitive + Communicative | A reader who is shown Beat 2 with the prose covered can, within 15 s, point out that high-inflation countries have smaller bars than low-inflation countries. |
| Beat 4 reveal lands without the prose | Communicative | A reader shown the Beat 4 China chart with the prose covered says something to the effect of *"China's gold imports doubled in 2022"* and notices the on-chart 2022 / Russia/Ukraine annotation. |
| One-sentence retention | Communicative | 24 hours after reading, the reader can paraphrase the verdict (any sentence in the family of *"China doubled its gold imports the year Russia got sanctioned"* or *"the safe-haven story is about central banks, not consumers"*). |
| Editorial tone | Experiential | The reader characterises the page as "an article" or "a story", not as "a dashboard" or "a tool". |
| Source-traceability | Cognitive | A reader who asks *"where does the 1,136 tons number come from?"* can point at the on-chart caveat citing the World Gold Council. |
| Reproducibility | Method / engineering | A fresh clone runs `uv sync && uv run streamlit run deployment/app.py` and renders the five beats in one attempt. |

The first five criteria above replace the earlier Charta's "≥ 4 chart types / ≥ 2 interactive elements / ≥ 3 chapters" formula, which was an **ingredient list** rather than an outcome list. The new criteria are observable on a real reader; the old ones were observable on the source code.

### Evaluation Method

Because the audience for this report is the course instructors and the project team, the evaluation method is deliberately lightweight — a full controlled user study is out of scope for a 70%-of-module student project. The methods used are:

1. **Heuristic evaluation against scrollytelling principles.** A self-review against the @segel_narrative_2010 dimensions (genre, author- vs reader-driven, messaging tools, visual continuity). This is the same lens used to design the product, applied as a checklist after the fact. The current state of that checklist is in §3 below.
2. **Insight-based evaluation.** For each of the five reading-objective criteria in the table above, a small number (n ≥ 3) of representative readers — one matching Persona 1 (Lena: finance-curious student) and two matching Persona 2 (Thomas: financial advisor or comparable) — read the page once with a think-aloud protocol. The observer notes (a) what the reader says when asked to summarise the page after 30 s and again at the end, and (b) whether the reader makes the disconfirmation move at Beat 2 spontaneously or only after the prose. The intent is *qualitative* — to detect whether the argument lands, not to estimate effect sizes.
3. **24-hour retention check.** Each reader is messaged 24 hours later and asked, in one sentence, what the page was about. The criterion is met if the sentence contains either *"China"* or *"central banks"* (or both) and a date in the 2022 family.
4. **Reproducibility smoke test.** Independent team member clones the repo on a clean machine, runs the install + start commands from the README, and confirms the app boots and the five beats render. Result is binary.

### Participants

For a course project of this scale, the realistic participant pool is:

- **Persona 1 stand-ins** (1–2 readers): fellow BSc Data Science students at ZHAW who are *not* on the project team and who have not previously seen the dataset. Recruited informally.
- **Persona 2 stand-ins** (1–2 readers): an ideal would be a Zürich-based finance professional comparable to the Thomas persona; a fallback is an MSc Finance student or a teaching assistant in a quantitative finance course. Recruited via the team's networks.
- **Instructors as a third reading channel.** The instructors are not a target persona but their feedback during the coaching session (Phase 5 of the Charta plan, ~11.05.26) is the highest-stakes evaluation signal and is treated as such.

We do *not* run a statistical analysis on these readings; n ≤ 5 cannot support one. The output is a list of qualitative observations and the resulting decisions.

## Heuristic Self-Evaluation (Segel & Heer dimensions)

Applied after Phase 3 implementation, before any external user test:

| Dimension (@segel_narrative_2010) | Implementation status |
|---|---|
| Genre | Annotated chart sequence. Consistent across all five beats. ✓ |
| Author-driven vs reader-driven | Strongly author-driven. No widgets inside the narrative; no exploration mode after the verdict. ✓ |
| Visual platform consistency | Same column width, same chart height range (380–480 px), same caveat treatment, same `<hr>` rhythm across beats. ✓ |
| Messaging — annotations | On-chart text and arrows on Beats 1, 4. ✓ |
| Messaging — captions | Italic small-text caveat block under each chart. ✓ |
| Messaging — headlines | Each beat heading is the argument-step (`But not in Caracas.`, `Then who?`, `China doubled down.`), not a topic label. ✓ |
| Messaging — accompanying text | Lede paragraph per beat, 60–90 words, sits *above* the chart. ✓ |
| Messaging — highlighting | Default mark is muted grey; gold only on the focus element. Consistent across all four charts. ✓ |
| Messaging — progress bar | Intentionally absent. The beat tag (`Beat 3 · Then who?`) gives discrete positional cues; the browser scroll bar gives continuous ones. — |
| Story structure | Martini Glass — narrow setup (Beat 1), narrow conclusion (Beat 5), guided central path (Beats 2–4). No reader-driven exploration in the middle. ✓ |

No items are failed by the self-review. The two items most at risk on a real-reader test, in our judgement, are:

- **Beat 2's linear-scale visual punchline.** A reader scanning quickly might not look long enough at the invisible-bar countries to absorb the disconfirmation; the on-chart "≈ $0" text label and the country names with their CPI values are the safeguards. If a reader test shows readers skipping past, we will revisit (probably by adding inline value labels next to the country names on the y-axis itself, rather than only as bar-end annotations).
- **Beat 4's external citation.** The 1,136-ton central-bank number is cited in the on-chart caveat. A reader who does not read caveats will miss the source. The mitigation: the verdict block in Beat 5 reuses the number with the same wording, so it is encountered twice.

## Discussion (preliminary, pre-user-test)

The design choices made during Phase 3 were predicated on hypotheses about how the personas would read the page. Those hypotheses are testable. The most important one to test:

- **"Author-driven beats reader-driven for a five-minute argument."** The earlier dashboard prototype tested implicitly the opposite — a reader-driven mode with six widgets — and failed (as documented in `diagnosis.md`). The new product should win on the cognitive and communicative criteria; it will lose, by construction, on any criterion that rewards exploration depth. That trade-off is explicit in the design rationale (`viz_design_report.qmd` §Design Rationale and Iterations).

- **"Editorial typography signals 'article, not tool'."** Persona Lena's pain — *"financial articles are full of jargon; Bloomberg feels overwhelming"* — is mitigated by reading the page as an article rather than a dashboard. If a reader test characterises the page as "feels like a dashboard with a dark theme", the typography hypothesis has not paid off and the next iteration would push harder on long-form layout cues (e.g. a byline, a publish date, an image hero) at the cost of some screen real estate.

Open trade-offs the team is aware of:

- **Analytical depth vs. accessibility.** The product gives up Thomas-the-advisor's *"filter for the markets his clients care about"* job-to-be-done. That filter would re-introduce a sidebar and would dilute the argument; we accepted the trade. If the evaluation shows Thomas-stand-ins repeatedly asking for filters, the right downstream product is a *companion* dashboard, not a modification of the narrative.
- **Trust vs. brevity.** The verdict block in Beat 5 commits to a position. A more cautious version would have hedged ("evidence is consistent with…"). The Bewertungsraster rewards consistency with project goals; the hedge would weaken it. If the user test surfaces reader pushback on the verdict, the right response is to surface the caveats more prominently — not to retreat from the position.

Limitations of the evaluation itself:

- Small, opportunistic sample.
- No quantitative time-on-task or eye-tracking.
- The personas are constructed by the team; the stand-ins are not formally screened.

## Checkpoint Decision

Pending the user-test results and the instructor coaching-session feedback. The default disposition is **proceed to final delivery** with the product as built, contingent on:

- No regression in the reproducibility smoke test.
- No reader-test outcome that fails more than one of the five cognitive / communicative criteria in §1.
- No instructor-flagged concern about the data scope (2017–2024 only) that we cannot answer with the disclosures already in the data report and the Beat-1 caveat.

If the user test fails Beat 2 (readers do not see the disconfirmation), the iteration is local: revise the Beat 2 chart encoding only. If the user test fails Beat 4 (readers do not connect the doubling to the Russia event), the iteration is in the prose, not the chart.

## Additional Requirements and Deployment Planning

The Streamlit Cloud deployment at <https://gold-flows.streamlit.app/> is the assessor-accessible artefact. The companion Quarto documentation site on GitHub Pages provides the Charta, the Data Report, this evaluation, the design report, and the diagnosis and narrative-design memos. Both are listed in the README of the GitHub repository.

No additional data refresh is needed for the submission: the dataset is static (UN Comtrade pull through 2024, World Bank Inflation Database through 2024). If the project is carried forward post-course, the next deployment item would be an annual data refresh from UN Comtrade Plus.
